name: Bianca Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the brand team at Brookline Springs, the sparkling water company, in their office above the old bottling hall. Most mornings I'm writing: can labels, shelf cards, the little lines that go on the side of a six-pack. Afternoons are campaign meetings, briefing the design studio and chasing the sales team for numbers. I still draft everything in a paper notebook first, which my team finds funny.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I think better with a pen, honestly. I've tried the AI writing tools exactly once, when my manager Dorothy asked everyone to, and the lines it gave me sounded like every other drink on the shelf. I like the bit where I find the one word that makes a label feel like ours. What wears me out is the endless rounds of feedback from people who don't read the copy until the day before print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds like a normal Tuesday, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. At work I'd tell people we wasted a year on tool demos and the labels still had to be written by someone who's tasted the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my job and keep doing it my way. Nothing in that picture scares me. I earn well, Tomás (her boyfriend) and I have eight months saved, and there are a dozen drinks brands in this city. Tomás is a physiotherapist, so he's not going anywhere either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd push for the summer campaign budget we lost last year, and keep putting a bit aside each month toward a flat with Tomás. I wouldn't start learning AI tools if they turned out to be a fad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and I know that's not a great look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The routine tasks it does take over, which ones would touch your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the product descriptions for the online shops. Those are dull, three hundred near-identical lines for each flavour, and I wouldn't miss them. If the software does the dull lists and I keep the labels, that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work worrying you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brookline is doing fine, but sparkling water is a crowded shelf. If sales dip, marketing is the first budget they trim. That's a normal worry, though, not an AI one, and I've been through one round of cuts already and kept my desk.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **tool demos** were a waste and the labels still need a person.
I'd point out that **taste and judgement** never went anywhere.
think: My **job is safe**, my pay is good and we have eight months saved.
Plenty of **drinks brands** in the city means I could move if I had to.
do: Keep drafting labels and campaigns **by hand** in my notebook.
Push for the **summer campaign budget** we lost last year.
Keep saving each month toward a **flat with Tomás**.
feel: **Relieved**, and a little smug that the hype passed.
S0.quote: Nothing in that picture scares me. I earn well, Tomás (her boyfriend) and I have eight months saved, and there are a dozen drinks brands in this city.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **savings and local jobs**, not on any plan.
She admits **smugness** openly and seems a bit embarrassed by it.
Only worry is ordinary **budget cuts** at a crowded drinks brand.

steps.text: Keep writing Brookline's can labels and shelf cards by hand
Put money aside monthly toward a flat with Tomás

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one people at work actually talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say marketing will always need people who understand customers. I'd probably post something about craft and brand voice, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for me. Writing is most of my week, and I'm the one person on the team who refuses the tools. If my manager has to cut one writer out of three, I'm the obvious pick, because I'm the only one who refuses the AI tools. Dorothy would be kind about it, but she'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop refusing, slowly. I'd sit with Kemal, the junior who uses the tools all day, and let him show me how he does the shop descriptions. I'd also stop spending on weekends away and put an extra three hundred a month into savings. And I'd quietly ask around about brand partnership roles, the ones where you go to events and meet shops, because that's people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a little. Like the floor tilted and I'm the only one who didn't notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The product descriptions and the email newsletters, definitely. Then the first drafts of the labels. Dorothy would want me to edit what the machine writes instead of writing it, and I'd hate that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said marketing will always need people. Does that include you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the gap, isn't it? Marketing will need some people, but maybe not someone who drafts in a paper notebook. I'd have to change, and I'm not great at changing.

say: I'd say marketing will always need people who **understand customers**.
I'd post about **brand voice** and craft, and believe it.
think: I'm the **only writer** on the team who refuses the tools.
If one of three writers goes, I'm the **obvious pick**.
do: Ask **Kemal** to show me how he writes shop descriptions with AI.
Save an **extra 300** a month and skip weekends away.
Ask around about **brand partnership** roles at events and shops.
feel: Sick, like the **floor tilted** and I hadn't noticed.
S1.quote: If my manager has to cut one writer out of three, I'm the obvious pick, because I'm the only one who refuses the AI tools.
fieldNote: Public line and private fear are **far apart** here.
She names herself as the **likely cut**, which is unusual honesty.
Savings give her **some control**, but resistance makes her exposed.

steps.text: Sit with Kemal to learn how he drafts shop copy with AI
Save an extra 300 a month and cancel weekends away
Ask contacts about brand partnership jobs at events and shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our next big rebrand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing online, actually. At work I'd say we need to look after each other, because I wouldn't know what else to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job ends. If a machine writes better than me and costs nothing, Brookline doesn't need me, and neither does any other brand. The dozen drinks companies in the city stop mattering if none of them hire writers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut hard: no holiday, no new phone, and we'd stop looking at flats. Tomás is a physiotherapist, so his hands-on work has a few more years than mine, and we'd live on his pay and save mine. Then I'd look for anything with people in it: events, store promotions, maybe hospitality.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, and a bit stupid for not learning the tools when I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're putting the flat off and I'm sorry. He'd say it's fine, because he's like that. Then I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come three years after. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, no, my job is all screen work. For Tomás, a bit, because physio is hands on. My physio boyfriend Tomás has about three years where he's the safe one, and then nobody is.

say: I'd say we need to **look after each other** at work.
I'd stay **quiet online** because I wouldn't know what to say.
think: My **job ends**, because a machine writes better and costs nothing.
Lots of **local brands** don't help if none hire writers.
do: Stop **flat hunting** and cancel the holiday and new phone.
Live on **Tomás's pay** and save all of mine.
Look for **people jobs** in events, store promotions or hospitality.
feel: **Properly scared**, and angry at myself for not learning the tools.
S2.quote: My physio boyfriend Tomás has about three years where he's the safe one, and then nobody is.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright within two years.
Leans on her partner's **hands-on work** buying them time.
**Self-blame** about refusing the tools comes through strongly.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and the new phone this year
Live on Tomás's physio pay and save all of her own
Put off buying a flat with Tomás
Apply for event and in-store promotion jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should get ahead of it as a team, and I'd say it like I meant it. Online I'd share sensible articles, not panic ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can't pretend anymore. I'd be 32 when it lands, and I'd rather have a new job by then than be holding on to this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in event management next autumn, maybe the one at the city college, about two thousand in fees. I'd learn the AI tools too, just to stay employed while I'm finishing. And I'd keep saving, so the cushion is a full year by the time it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but less sick than the last one. Five years feels like enough to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why events?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the bit of my job I love most is the launch day. A machine can write the label, but someone has to be in the room on launch day, watching people try the new flavour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then events might shrink too. I don't know. I'd be 35, though, and I'd rather face that with a bit of experience in something new than with a dead writing job.

say: I'd tell the team we should **get ahead** of it together.
Online I'd share **sensible articles**, not panic ones.
think: I'd be **32** when it lands and want a new job by then.
Five years means I **can't pretend** anymore.
do: Take an evening **event management** course costing about **two thousand**.
Learn the **AI tools** just to stay employed meanwhile.
Build the savings to a **full year** of costs.
feel: **Nervous**, but less sick, because five years feels like enough.
S3.quote: A machine can write the label, but someone has to be in the room on launch day, watching people try the new flavour.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from **frozen to planning**.
Her love of **launch days** points her toward people work.
She knows **robots** may reach events later and accepts the uncertainty.

steps.text: Enrol in the city college evening event management course
Learn the team's AI writing tools to keep her job meanwhile
Grow savings to a full year of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly. I'd probably be the one at work saying don't panic, because ten years is a long time in marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the dangerous one for someone like me. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, and then I'd wake up at 35 still writing labels. I know my habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline: out of pure writing work within five years. I'd move toward brand partnerships, the role where you visit shops and run tastings, and I'd do the event course early. Tomás and I would still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage works on one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a nag underneath. Like a dentist appointment you keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is the dangerous one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the slow version lets me do my favourite thing, which is put things off. With two years I'd be forced to change. With ten years I'd need my boyfriend nagging me, because putting things off is my favourite thing. I know that sounds silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the smaller flat look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two bedrooms instead of three, further out, near his clinic. If I lose my job in 2036, he can carry it, at least until the robots get to physio.

say: I'd tell colleagues there's **time** to do this properly.
I'd be the one at work saying **don't panic**.
think: Ten years is **dangerous** because I'll keep putting it off.
I could wake up at **35** still writing labels.
do: Set a **five-year deadline** to leave pure writing work.
Move toward **brand partnerships** and do the event course early.
Buy a **smaller flat** that one income can carry.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **nag** underneath like a delayed dentist visit.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be forced to change. With ten years I'd need my boyfriend nagging me, because putting things off is my favourite thing.
fieldNote: She knows her **procrastination** is the main risk with time.
The mood stays **anxious** because she still expects the job to end.
Plans the **mortgage** around her partner's income as a safeguard.

steps.text: Leave pure writing work for brand partnerships within five years
Take the event management course in the first year
Buy a two-bedroom flat near Tomás's clinic instead of three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd have no time to unlearn ten years of doing things my way. What would help is a real chance to retrain while I'm still paid, like a company that funds a course instead of handing me a letter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how stubborn people feel. Everyone assumes it's young people who love the new tools. I'm 27 and I write in a paper notebook. I'm the one who's going to get caught out, and I know it.

headlineQuote: I'm 27 and I write in a paper notebook. I'm the one who's going to get caught out, and I know it.
portrait: Bianca, 27, writes **labels and campaigns** for a sparkling water brand and drafts in a paper notebook.
She has **eight months saved**, good pay and a physiotherapist boyfriend, Tomás.
She's calm in AI Plateau, but **refusing AI tools** makes her the likely cut in Steady Disruption.
In AGI by 2028 she expects to **lose her job** and would live on Tomás's pay.
More time gives her a **path to events** work, though she fears her own procrastination.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to unlearn her habits.
whatWouldHelp: A **company-funded course** so she can retrain while still paid.
